Hi Sidney,

To investigate problems with using a sleeplog in GGIR it is best to start with trying to read the sleeplog first with GGIR function g.loadlog only.

For example:
sleeplog = g.loadlog(loglocation="C:/mysleeplog.csv",coln1=2, colid=1,nnights=7,sleeplogidnum=FALSE)
print(head(sleeplog))

If this already leads to warnings it may indicate that either the sleeplog is not in the right format or the arguments like colid, coln1, or sleeplogidnum are not correctly specified.

If this does not lead to warnings then it may be good to double check that the ID numbers in the sleeplog file match the ID numbers in the GGIR part2_summary.csv report.

Best wishes,
Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Hello Abby,

Cuong Ngo <https://www.math.ku.dk/english/staff/?pure=en/persons/626026> contacted me a while ago about using GGIR algorithms in Whales. I am not sure whether he was using GGIR or had his own software implementation.

Either way, I think you could use GGIR part 1 and 2 for any organism or even non-living objects to describe their acceleration and estimate their orientation.Maybe start with the functionality related to arguments ilevels, qlevels, and qwindow.

The sleep detection in GGIR part 3 and 4 should also work well if you figure out an optimal setting for the angle and time threshold of the algorithm. However, the underlyig assumption is that the species sleep/wakes with 24 hour rhythm and that the main sleep period happens at night. It may not work well if used in species that sleep/wake with alternative rhythms or who are awake at night and have their main sleep period in the middle of the day.

Note that the auto-calibration function in GGIR part 1 works best if the sensor is kept still from time to time in wide range of orientations relative to the horizontal plane. For human behaviour this is no problem, but if you are studying an animal that never rotates relative to the horizontal plane then that could be tricky. In that case I would recommend not using the acceleration metrics that rely on knowledge about gravity (ENMO, EN, ENMOa, LFENMO, HFENplus). Instead, you may want to use BFEN which also is a good indicator of the magnitude of acceleration and is easy to explain as it has been used for decades across scientific fields. Although not under the name BFEN but the concept of band-pass filtering is well established.

Finally, I know that Cassim Ladha has been specialising in animal tracking and is CEO of a company that offers services on this: https://vetsens.co.uk/. I am almost certain he does not use GGIR, but you may want to reach out to him for feedback.

Thanks,
Vincent

You are providing some of the arguments such as threshold.lig twice, make sure that you provide every argument only once.

Hi Kerstin,

See my answers below:

in the file plots_to_check_data_quality_1.pdf: at what time does Day start, i.e. the marked starting point 0, 1, 2 etc. on the x-axis?

The tick mark on the axis for each day is midnight as these plots are made during the earlier stages of GGIR and are therefore midnight-midnight summaries of the data as per part 2 outputs

in the file visualization_sleep.pdf: what does the colour yellow/lime signify?

Information for this can be found here: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/GGIR.html#5_Motivation_and_clarification in the 4.2 Output part 4, then on the 4.2.3 visualisation_sleep.pdf tab just underneath. Pasted in the description anyway for you:
"Explanation of the image: Each line represents one night. Colours are used to distinguish definitions of sustained inactivity bouts (2 definitions in this case) and to indicate existence or absence of overlap with the sleeplog. When argument outliers.only is set to FALSE it will visualise all available nights in the dataset. If outliers.only is set to TRUE it will visualise only nights with a difference in onset or waking time between sleeplog and sustained inactivity bouts larger than the value of argument criterror.
This visualisation with outliers.only set to TRUE and critererror set to 4 was very powerful to identify entry errors in sleeplog data in van Hees et al PLoSONE 2015. We had over 25 thousand nights of data, and this visualisation allowed us to quickly zoom in on the most problematic nights to investigate possible mistakes in GGIR or mistakes in data entry."
Hope that helps,
Ben
